extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; readers interested in philosophy, death, and moral reflection
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted passages from Montaigne's Essays (chapters on fear, happiness judged after death, and studying philosophy as preparation for death). The text gives normative claims and practical prescriptions about how to regard fear, fortune, and death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness cannot be judged until after death
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That men are not to judge of our happiness till after death.’ Happiness should not be attributed during life because fortune is uncertain and may change a person’s condition; the last day of life is the true test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Croesus crying 'O Solon' on the scaffold; Agesilaus' reply about Priam; many historical reversals (kings becoming prisoners or men of high station dying miserably). The final act (‘the master-day’) reveals the truth of a life and can remove or confer reputation (Scipio, Epaminondas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Death is the final assay of a life — dying well redeems a life
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner of one's death can give a good or ill repute to the whole life; one should be judged by how one bears the last scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites examples of infamous men who died composedly and of great men whose end ruined their renown. Aim to 'die well' — patiently and tranquilly — because the end colors prior actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ascribe lasting felicity to present fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortune is mutable and greatness may be overturned quickly; apparent successes during life do not prove lasting happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical anecdotes (Pompey, Ludovico Sforza, Mary Queen of Scots, successors to Alexander reduced to menial jobs) illustrate how rapidly conditions change; therefore reserve judgment about a person's happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: To study philosophy is to prepare oneself to die
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying philosophy withdraws the soul from bodily attachment and trains one to contemn death; philosophy’s end is to teach not to fear dying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cicero quoted: study is apprenticeship to death. Philosophical contemplation makes us familiar with separation of soul and body and aims to produce tranquility and contentment rather than technical disputation for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: The pursuit of virtue is itself pleasurable and preferable to base pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: All schools agree that pleasure is the end, but the nobler pleasure is the pursuit and practice of virtue — more robust, lasting, and ennobling than mean pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne distinguishes pleasures: perfect pleasure accompanies virtue and its pursuit is part of felicity; difficulties in attaining virtue ennoble rather than detract from it. Reject the notion that virtue’s cost outweighs its fruit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt of death is a chief benefit of virtue and grants liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning to die removes subjection and gives a soft, easy tranquillity; if one rightly comprehends death as no evil, nothing in life can truly oppress him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premeditation of death is equated to premeditation of liberty: one who has learned to die has 'unlearned to serve.' Anecdote: Paulus Emilius' reply about a prisoner in a triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disarm death’s novelty by frequent reflection and familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Make death commonplace in thought and imagination so its strangeness and terror are removed — represent it often and in varied shapes to fortify oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical suggestions: at small accidents imagine 'and what if it had been death itself?'; Egyptians brought a dried skeleton into feasts as a memento; constantly speaking of death and reflecting upon it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premeditation of death lessens its terror and readies one for it
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeatedly contemplating death makes the idea familiar and reduces initial sting so one may face death with less disturbance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne reports that imagining death often removes its power; when sick one often feels less terror than when healthy because nature and progressive decline prepare the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be practically prepared for death: settle affairs and keep a will
rubrics_metrics.description: One should be ready at all times to die by keeping one’s affairs in order and being 'booted and spurred' — avoid postponing necessary preparations until death is imminent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of vulgar avoidance of thinking about wills until the physician has given up; anecdote of a memorandum written while a league from home because one cannot be certain of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid projects that require long completion or excessive desire for completion
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not attach oneself passionately to enterprises that require long time to finish, because death may interrupt them and cause grief; prefer to be engaged in life’s activities without over-attachment to long projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: design nothing requiring excessive time to finish; be born to action and accept works left incomplete. Examples: complaints of men who die before victories, marriages, or completing works such as chronicles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and study the deaths of others as instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting and reflecting on the various manners of people's deaths (their words, looks, and bearing) is a useful exercise to learn to die and thus to live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne says he would compile a register of deaths and references Dicarchus' similar undertaking; learning from others' ends teaches how to face one’s own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use societal practices to accustom people to death (public sepulture, spectacles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate communal exposure to death (burials near churches, public funeral rites) so that people, including children, are not startled by corpses and come to accept mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lycurgus' practice of placing sepultures in frequented city places; old customs of enlivening banquets with spectacles of slaughter to familiarize people with death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear is the most oppressive passion and often worse than death
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear, more than any other passion, can exceed the trouble of other accidents and may be a worse torment than death itself; it deprives reason and can lead to madness or self-destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pompey's friends at his murder who could not grieve until fear passed; soldiers who, panicked, threw themselves on the enemy; people who have killed themselves to escape perpetual alarms of fear. Fear can drive men to valiant despair or paralysing cowardice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear deprives the mind of reason and duty and distorts judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear can expel intelligence and good counsel from the mind, leading to rash or self-defeating behaviour; once a good sound fear is conceived, one will not withstand the enemy or danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited lines: 'Then fear drove out all intelligence from my mind.' Historical episodes (Emperor Theophilus stunned in battle; Roman troops under Sempronius) illustrate how fear removes sense and causes disastrous acts.
